newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish parliament eases abortion law in final vote.
newsitem.headline: Polish parliament eases abortion law in final vote.

text.p: The lower house of Poland's parliament voted on Thursday to overthrow a Senate veto and pass a bill liberalising the country's tough anti-abortion law -- a change strongly opposed by the Roman Catholic Church.
Deputies voted by 228 to 195 with 16 abstentions in favour of the bill, which ex-communist President Aleksander Kwasniewski has promised to sign into law.

The measure allows women to end pregnancies before the 12th week if they faced financial or personal problems, but only after counselling and a period of reflection, and also provides for sex education in schools and cheaper contraception.

Under the existing law, passed in 1993 by a pro-Catholic government, abortions are now allowed only if a pregnancy threatens a woman's life or health, results from incest or rape, or when the foetus is irreparably damaged.

The bill, first passed by the lower house in August, was vetoed by the Senate early this month and its backers in the lower house, the Sejm, needed to muster 50 percent plus one of the votes to reject the upper house veto.

The Church, drawing on the authority of Polish-born Pope John Paul, organised a huge protest campaign against what it sees as a licence to kill unborn children, culminating in a march in Warsaw on Wednesday by more than 30,000 people.
Bishops had issued a last-minute appeal in a letter to deputies, begging them to "Stand in defence of life."
"The situation is very grim -- that parliament reacted this way," priest Marian Subocz, deputy secretary-general of the Catholic Episcopate, said after the vote.

"Many people in Poland were demanding protection for the unborn child. The Church will continue as before to defend life and help mothers who are in a difficult situation," he told Reuters. "Killing of life that has started is a great evil."

The reform was backed by the main ruling coalition party, the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD) and some liberal or left-leaning opposition deputies, who argued that abortion was widely available in underground clinics or neighbouring countries and the new law would end much misery.
Much of the SLD's smaller Peasant party coalition partner sided with right-leaning opposition groups in opposing the bill, which was strongly fought by parties grouped around the Solidarity union.

Opinion polls suggest that opposition to easier abortion has risen in recent years, and that Polish society, of which 90 percent is at least nominally Catholic, is about equally divided over the emotive issue.
